rows.verified: Construction work must be conducted without putting members of the public or other affected workers at risk.
Construction sites require measures to manage access across defined boundaries and exclude unauthorised people.
Site boundaries should be physically defined with suitable fencing or hoarding where necessary and maintained throughout the work.
Materials and tools should be controlled so they cannot fall outside the site boundary and injure the public.
Excavations, manholes, stairwells and open edges that could affect the public need barriers or secure covers.
Vehicles and plant should be isolated, immobilised and secured when sites are left unattended where necessary.
Building materials should be stored so they cannot topple, roll or otherwise create danger beyond the work area.
Site security arrangements should take particular account of children and other vulnerable people who may be attracted to construction sites.
The necessary boundary and public-protection controls depend on the work, neighbourhood, adjacent land use, visitors and vulnerable groups.
Construction public-protection evidence is site- and project-specific and is not an exact parcel-level trespass or injury probability.
Employers must provide welfare facilities and a working environment that is healthy and safe for everyone, including disabled workers.
Workers must have access to toilets, handwashing, drinking water, clothing storage and places to rest and eat meals.
A healthy workplace should have suitable ventilation, lighting, room, seating, cleanliness and waste arrangements.
Toilets and washing facilities should be sufficient, accessible, clean, ventilated, lit and supplied with water, soap and hand drying.
Construction workers must have access to toilets and facilities for washing, changing, eating and rest from the start of the project.
Construction washing facilities should be positioned near toilets and changing areas and provide suitable water, cleaning and drying facilities.
Visiting delivery and collection drivers must have safe and easy access to toilets and handwashing facilities at worksites.
Walkways to welfare facilities should be marked, signposted and protected from vehicle incursion.
The type, number and location of welfare facilities depend on workforce size, disability needs, work type, hazards, remoteness and working patterns.
Welfare evidence is workplace- and workforce-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health-readiness probability.
